title: Mutualism or antagonism? Effects of funnel-web spiders (Lycosidae) and vegetation cover on plant herbivory, growth, and fruit production in Hohenbergia catingae (Bromeliaceae) in the Caatinga
content:
Abstract
Species interactions can range from mutualistic to antagonistic, with outcomes that are influenced by biotic and abiotic factors. Little is known about interactions between bromeliads and spiders in the Caatinga, a highly diverse and threatened dry forest ecosystem. Here, we explored the relationship between the bromeliad Hohenbergia catingae and the funnel-web spider Aglaoctenus lagotis, including the potential influence of vegetation cover. Over the course of nine sampling events (2023–2025), we monitored 41 plants for the presence of spider webs, herbivory, and growth; we surveyed 10 additional plants to characterize fruit production. Key metrics included leaf growth, herbivore abundance and richness, levels of herbivory, and fruit production. Our results revealed that the presence of spider webs was uncorrelated with herbivore abundance or levels of herbivory but that plants with webs exhibited diminished leaf growth and reduced fruit production, probably because spiders deterred pollinators. Vegetation cover appeared to influence the presence of spiders on plants. However, vegetation cover did not seem to shape plant–spider interactions. Our findings suggest that these interactions could be parasitic instead of mutualistic—spiders might negatively affect bromeliad performance without protecting against herbivores.
